name: Lebanon

facts.religion: Muslim about 67% (Shia and Sunni), Christian about 32%, Druze

system_note: Power is shared by religious sect under a confessional system.
snapshot: Lebanon was dragged back into war when Hezbollah fired on Israel after the strikes on Iran, wrecking the new government's year of reclaiming sovereignty.
culture: Beirut has long been the Arab world's publishing, nightlife and fashion capital, and Lebanese cuisine, from mezze to manakish, is loved worldwide. Fairuz's songs play every morning across the region. The country's 18 recognised religious sects shape marriage, schooling and politics. The Lebanese diaspora, larger than the population at home, is a lifeline.
society: A 2019 financial collapse wiped out savings and pushed most people into poverty, and the 2020 Beirut port explosion killed over 200 people. The state shares power by sect: the president is Maronite Christian, the prime minister Sunni and the speaker Shia. Lebanon hosts more than a million Syrian refugees.
situation: For 40 years Hezbollah, founded with Iranian help during Israel's 1982 invasion, was Lebanon's state within a state: a militia stronger than the national army and a party that could block any government. The 2024 war with Israel broke much of that power. Its leader Hassan Nasrallah was killed, a new president, former army chief Joseph Aoun, and a reformist prime minister, Nawaf Salam, took office, and the government formally committed to disarming it. 2026 was supposed to be the year Lebanon reclaimed its sovereignty. Instead it was pulled back into war.

When the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February, Hezbollah fired on Israel in solidarity, and Israel resumed heavy bombing of Beirut's southern suburbs and the south from early March (RANE). Salam's government, furious that Hezbollah had dragged the country in, voted again to ban the group's military activities, but the army, which had spent months clearing weapons south of the Litani River largely with Hezbollah's consent, has no appetite to confront it by force (Fox News). The cost was democratic too. Parliamentary elections set for May, seen as the best chance since 2005 to break the old sectarian parties' grip, did not happen: parliament extended its own term by two years, to 2028, citing the war (GlobalSecurity). US envoy Tom Barrack had warned that postponing the vote "would ignite major chaos." Lebanon is still recovering from a 2019 financial collapse that wiped out ordinary savings and the 2020 Beirut port explosion.
power: A confessional parliamentary republic. By convention the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker a Shia Muslim; parliament's 128 seats are split equally between Christians and Muslims. Speaker Nabih Berri, Hezbollah's ally, has held his post since 1992.
holders: President Joseph Aoun, since January 2025; Prime Minister Nawaf Salam.
